exam: Define qSOFA and list its components. — qSOFA is a rapid bedside screening tool for sepsis; it includes respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mental status (GCS ≤13), and systolic BP ≤100 mmHg.
What score on qSOFA triggers urgent evaluation? — A score of 2 or more signals high risk and mandates immediate assessment, possible transfer, and early treatment.

A patient with pneumonia has RR 24, SBP 98 mmHg, confused. What is the qSOFA score and next step? — Score = 3; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg fluids, and arrange ICU or higher‑level care.
Why is qSOFA preferred over SIRS in low‑resource hospitals? — qSOFA needs no labs, uses only bedside vitals, and better predicts mortality, making it feasible where labs are limited.
How does chronic hypertension affect interpretation of SBP ≤100 mmHg? — Patients may maintain SBP >100 mmHg despite shock; consider a drop of >40 mmHg from baseline as concerning.

Explain why lactate measurement improves sepsis detection even when qSOFA is low. — Elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L) indicates tissue hypoperfusion and predicts mortality, identifying patients who need aggressive resuscitation despite a low qSOFA.

A febrile child has RR 30, normal mental status, BP normal. How does this affect qSOFA? — Only respiratory rate is abnormal; qSOFA score = 1, so it does not trigger high‑risk pathway, but child‑specific sepsis criteria must still be applied.
What alternative vasopressor can be used if norepinephrine is unavailable? — Dopamine can be used, titrated to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg, but it has more arrhythmic risk.
How to assess mental status for qSOFA in a patient on chronic antipsychotics? — Compare current GCS to baseline; any new confusion or drop to ≤13 counts as altered mental status.
What limitation does qSOFA have in malaria‑endemic areas? — Severe malaria can cause tachypnea and hypotension without bacterial infection, leading to false‑positive qSOFA scores.
List the bedside steps to measure respiratory rate accurately. — Observe patient for 30 seconds, count breaths, multiply by 2; ensure patient is at rest and not talking.
When should you repeat the qSOFA assessment? — After initial resuscitation (fluids, antibiotics) and every 2‑4 hours in unstable patients to track response.
What is the first antimicrobial choice for community‑acquired sepsis in Kenya? — A third‑generation cephalosporin plus coverage for Staphylococcus aureus; adjust later based on cultures.

Why avoid excessive crystalloid after initial 30 mL/kg in septic shock? — Large volumes can cause pulmonary edema and abdominal compartment syndrome, especially in patients with cardiac or renal failure.

b: Ask about recent fever, chills, cough, dysuria, wound discharge, or abdominal pain – any new or worsening symptom within 48 h.
Inquire about chronic conditions (HIV, TB, diabetes, hypertension, renal or liver disease) that may mask vital changes.
Ask about medication use (antihypertensives, steroids, antipsychotics, traditional herbs) that can alter blood pressure or mental status.
Determine recent fluid intake, vomiting, diarrhoea or bleeding that may affect volume status.
Establish baseline mental status (orientation, speech, mobility) to detect new confusion.
sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and rapid exam allow you to calculate qSOFA and identify the infection source while recognising confounders common in low‑resource settings.

b: Full blood count – leukocytosis or left shift supports infection; neutropenia may mask typical response.
Serum creatinine – rise ≥0.3 mg/dL or ≥1.5× baseline indicates renal dysfunction; if unavailable, monitor urine output.
Serum bilirubin – >2 mg/dL suggests hepatic involvement; if lab not present, look for jaundice or encephalopathy.
Lactate – >2 mmol/L signals tissue hypoperfusion; if lactate unavailable, rely on persistent hypotension or mottled skin.
Arterial blood gas – PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg indicates respiratory failure; if ABG not possible, use SpO₂ <94 % on room air as surrogate.
sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use readily available tests to confirm infection, assess organ dysfunction and guide resuscitation; have alternatives when labs are missing.

b: Sepsis: infection plus organ dysfunction (SOFA increase ≥2) – qSOFA ≥2 flags high risk and prompts full SOFA assessment.
Mild‑moderate sepsis: infection with qSOFA 0–1 and no hypotension; manage on general ward with close monitoring.
Severe sepsis (pre‑SOFA era): now encompassed by sepsis with organ dysfunction; use SOFA components to grade severity.
sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion, qSOFA score and organ‑dysfunction criteria to stage sepsis and decide on escalation.

b: Malaria: fever, tachypnoea, altered mental status; differentiate with rapid test and peripheral smear; treat malaria first if positive.
Severe anemia: low BP and tachycardia may mimic shock; check haemoglobin; transfuse if <7 g/dL in adults.
Pulmonary embolism: sudden dyspnoea, tachypnoea, hypotension; consider ECG, D‑dimer, bedside ultrasound; anticoagulate if confirmed.
Acute heart failure: dyspnoea, crackles, elevated JVP; assess for peripheral oedema, cardiac auscultation, POCUS; treat with diuretics if fluid overload.
sections.p: Several common diseases mimic qSOFA components; systematic comparison avoids misclassification.

t.b: Positive rapid test or smear points to malaria; if negative, pursue bacterial source; both may coexist.
Low haemoglobin with normal capillary refill suggests anemia; fluid challenge improves hypovolemia but not anemia.
Pleural rub, focal chest pain, and ECG changes favour embolism; infiltrate on X‑ray favours pneumonia.
Elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, S3 gallop suggest heart failure; septic shock shows warm extremities early, low JVP.

b: First things first: obtain airway, breathing, circulation; give high‑flow oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥94 % and place the patient in a supine position with legs slightly elevated.
Immediate empiric antibiotics: start broad‑spectrum agents covering Gram‑negative bacilli and Staphylococcus aureus; avoid narrow‑spectrum drugs until cultures are available.
Fluid resuscitation: give 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus; repeat if MAP remains <65 mmHg or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h.
Source control: obtain cultures, imaging, and perform drainage or surgery as indicated; do not delay antibiotics for imaging.
Monitoring: record qSOFA components every hour, track urine output, mental status, and vital signs; reassess need for additional fluids or vasopressors.
Escalation/referral: if qSOFA remains ≥2 after initial resuscitation, or if organ failure worsens, arrange transfer to higher‑level care or ICU.
sections.p: A systematic ladder guides rapid sepsis care while using qSOFA to trigger escalation, especially where laboratory support is limited.

b: Beta‑lactam antibiotics may cause hypersensitivity rash; stop the drug and switch to a non‑beta‑lactam if anaphylaxis occurs.
Vancomycin can cause nephrotoxicity; monitor creatinine and avoid concomitant aminoglycosides unless essential.
Fluoroquinolones may prolong QT; check baseline ECG if patient is on other QT‑prolonging agents or has electrolyte disturbances.
Dopamine at high doses increases risk of tachyarrhythmia; if arrhythmia develops, reduce dose or switch to norepinephrine.
Crystalloid overload can precipitate pulmonary edema; watch for rising respiratory rate, crackles, and falling SpO₂, then consider diuretics if fluid‑responsive shock resolves.
sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse effects and drug interactions prevents iatrogenic harm during sepsis resuscitation.

b: Acute kidney injury: rising creatinine or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h; start renal‑protective measures and consider dialysis referral.
Respiratory failure: PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg or increasing work of breathing; initiate non‑invasive ventilation or intubation and arrange ICU transfer.
Cardiovascular collapse: MAP <65 mmHg despite fluids and norepinephrine; add vasopressin or epinephrine and request critical care support.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation: falling platelets, rising PT/aPTT, schistocytes; give blood products as guided and treat underlying infection.
Lactate >4 mmol/L or rising trend despite therapy; indicates tissue hypoperfusion and mandates aggressive resuscitation and escalation.
sections.p: Sepsis can progress to organ dysfunction; early recognition of complications dictates transfer or higher‑level interventions.

b: HIV infection: opportunistic pathogens may present with atypical fever patterns; obtain broader cultures and consider antifungal coverage.
Tuberculosis: chronic cough and weight loss may lower respiratory rate; do not rely solely on qSOFA; obtain sputum GeneXpert if available.
Malnutrition: baseline low blood pressure and altered mental status are common; use clinical judgment and treat aggressively despite low qSOFA.
Pregnancy: physiological SBP may be lower; use MAP target ≥65 mmHg and avoid drugs harmful to fetus (e.g., tetracyclines).
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia can blunt fever response; monitor glucose and avoid high‑dose steroids unless indicated.
Alcohol use: withdrawal can raise respiratory rate and cause confusion; differentiate with CIWA‑Ar assessment and treat withdrawal concurrently.
Renal or hepatic failure: dose‑adjust antibiotics, avoid nephrotoxic agents, and monitor for accumulation of metabolites.
Age extremes: children have higher normal respiratory rates; elderly may have blunted tachycardia; adjust thresholds accordingly.
sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local conditions can mask or mimic qSOFA criteria, altering interpretation and treatment choices.

b: Pregnancy: give ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for intra‑abdominal sources; avoid aminoglycosides unless renal function is normal; maintain left lateral tilt.
Elderly: anticipate atypical presentations; start empiric antibiotics early and monitor for delirium; consider reduced fluid volumes if cardiac failure is present.
People with HIV: include coverage for Pneumocystis jirovecii (trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole) if CD4 <200; screen for cryptococcal antigen in meningitis suspicion.

Low‑resource settings: if lactate unavailable, repeat qSOFA after each intervention; use oral or intramuscular antibiotics when IV access delayed; rely on clinical fluid responsiveness (capillary refill, pulse pressure).
sections.p: Tailored approaches ensure safe sepsis care for vulnerable populations and low‑resource environments.

Why is qSOFA preferred over SIRS in low‑resource settings? — Uses only bedside signs, no labs, and predicts mortality better.

A febrile child has a respiratory rate of 30 but normal mental status and BP – how does this affect qSOFA? — Score remains 0; still assess for sepsis but do not trigger high‑risk pathway solely on rate.

A patient on chronic antipsychotics is confused; how to assess mental status for qSOFA? — Determine new change from baseline; if unchanged, do not count as altered.
What is the limitation of qSOFA in malaria‑endemic areas? — Malaria can cause high fever and tachypnea without bacterial infection, potentially inflating the score.
ai.title: qSOFA Score in Sepsis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The qSOFA is a rapid bedside tool to identify patients with suspected infection who are at risk of poor outcomes. It uses three simple clinical criteria and guides urgent assessment and management, especially where resources are limited.

b: Sepsis definition (Sepsis‑3): infection + acute organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2).
qSOFA is a screening tool, not a diagnostic test.
sections.p: Sepsis is life‑threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection. In low‑resource settings, early recognition is crucial because advanced monitoring may be unavailable.

b: Respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min
Altered mental status (Glasgow ≤13 or new confusion)
Systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg
sections.p: qSOFA uses three bedside variables that predict mortality and need for higher‑level care.

b: High‑risk patients need prompt antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and source control.
In settings without lactate measurement, qSOFA guides escalation.
sections.p: A qSOFA score of 2 or more signals high risk and should trigger urgent evaluation, possible transfer, and early sepsis bundle implementation.

t.b: Detect leukocytosis/leukopenia and anemia; guides infection severity and need for transfusion.
Identifies tissue hypoperfusion; >2 mmol/L supports sepsis diagnosis.
Identify causative organism; if unavailable, treat empirically based on local epidemiology.
Screen for urinary source, common in low‑resource settings.

b: Broad‑spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour; choose agents covering Gram‑negative bacilli, Staphylococcus aureus, and malaria/TB if clinically suspected.
30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate >2 mmol/L; repeat as needed.
Vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) if MAP <65 mmHg after fluids; consider dopamine if norepinephrine unavailable.
Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥94 %; consider CPAP if respiratory distress and no ventilator.
Frequent reassessment of qSOFA; a rising score mandates escalation.
sections.p: Treat the infection first, then support organ function while monitoring qSOFA components.

b: SOFA requires laboratory data (PaO₂/FiO₂, platelets, bilirubin, creatinine, MAP).
SIRS uses temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and WBC; less predictive of mortality.
sections.p: qSOFA is sometimes mixed up with the full SOFA score or with SIRS criteria.

b: Chronic hypertension may keep SBP >100 mmHg despite shock.
Baseline neurological impairment can obscure new mental status changes.
Hyperventilation from anxiety may raise respiratory rate without sepsis.
sections.p: Certain conditions can mask or mimic qSOFA components.

b: Always count respirations for 30 seconds and multiply by 2.
Check mental status using AVPU or GCS; note any new confusion.
Measure SBP with a cuff; low readings in a dehydrated child may be misleading.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to apply qSOFA quickly and to act on the result.

Signs of organ failure (e.g., oliguria, altered consciousness)
